section_summaries.epidemiology: Hookworm infects approximately 800 million people worldwide, predominantly in sub-Saharan Africa, Asia, and tropical regions of the Americas. It is soil-transmitted, with larvae penetrating exposed human skin. Transmission is favored by rural poverty, poor sanitation, specific soil types, high temperatures, and adequate moisture. Prevalence rises in early life and intensity often peaks in adulthood, particularly in women of reproductive age and the elderly. Strongyloidiasis has a patchy, widespread distribution in warm, wet, tropical, and subtropical areas, and in temperate regions with poor sanitation. An estimated 30-100 million people are infected globally, though prevalence is typically low (<10%). It is endemic in tropical Asia, Africa, Latin America, rural Appalachia, and parts of southern and eastern Europe, with elevated prevalence in older HTLV-1-infected patients, immigrants, travelers, or military veterans from endemic areas.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: For hookworm, ova are passed in feces, develop into infective third-stage larvae (L3) in the soil. L3 larvae penetrate exposed human skin (or are orally infective for A. duodenale), enter the venous circulation, migrate to the lungs, are coughed up and swallowed, then mature into adult worms in the small intestine. Adult hookworms lacerate intestinal capillaries, ingest blood, lyse red cells, and degrade hemoglobin, leading to chronic blood loss and iron-deficiency anemia (e.g., 25 N. americanus cause 1 mL blood loss/day). For Strongyloides, its complex life cycle involves host and soil stages and is unique for its ability to multiply within the host (autoinfection), leading to persistent infection. L3 larvae from contaminated soil penetrate skin, migrate through the lungs, are swallowed, and mature into adult females in the small intestine. Adult females lay eggs that hatch rapidly into rhabditiform larvae in the intestinal mucosa, which can either be passed in stool or transform into L3 in the gut, causing autoinfection. In immunocompromised individuals (e.g., due to corticosteroids or HTLV-1 co-infection), dysregulated autoinfection can lead to hyperinfection syndrome, characterized by massive larval dissemination, secondary bacteremias, and disseminated strongyloidiasis to ectopic sites.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: For hookworm, initial skin penetration causes "ground itch" (intense itching, papules) or cutaneous larva migrans (from animal hookworms). Larval migration through the lungs can cause cough, wheezing, and eosinophilic infiltrates. The intestinal phase involves epigastric pain and tenderness. The hallmark is chronic microcytic, hypochromic iron-deficiency anemia (IDA), leading to lassitude, weakness, apathy, depression, pallor, koilonychia, angular stomatitis, and chlorosis. IDA impairs growth and cognition in children and increases maternal morbidity and adverse birth outcomes in pregnant women. For Strongyloides, manifestations include acute infection (often asymptomatic, or with cough, wheezing, abdominal pain, diarrhea), chronic persisting infection (classic triad of larva currens, abdominal pain, and diarrhea), and hyperinfection syndrome. Hyperinfection is severe, with extensive gastrointestinal symptoms (pain, bloating, diarrhea, constipation, ileus), variable pulmonary symptoms, common larva currens, high mortality, and frequent complications like gram-negative enteric bacterial sepsis, meningitis, peritonitis, and endocarditis.
section_summaries.diagnosis: For hookworm, diagnosis is confirmed by identifying hookworm ova in stool specimens, especially in patients from endemic areas with anemia or eosinophilia. Direct fecal examination detects heavy infections, while concentration techniques (e.g., zinc sulfate flotation, formalin-ether) are used for lighter infections. Quantitative fecal egg counts (e.g., Kato-Katz) are used for epidemiological studies, but the method requires immediate evaluation. For Strongyloides, diagnosis requires diligent search for rhabditiform larvae in fecal specimens, particularly in at-risk individuals (HTLV-1 positive, on corticosteroids). Techniques to improve larval detection include nutrient agar cultures, Baermann funnel gauze concentration, and Harada Mori cultures. Serology, such as immunofluorescence antibody assays and ELISA tests, offers high specificity and sensitivity, though cross-reactivity with other nematodes and limited antigen availability are considerations.
section_summaries.treatment: For hookworm, oral anti-helminthics are the treatment, often administered in mass treatment programs. Benzimidazole agents like albendazole (400 mg single-dose, 72% cure rate) are first-line, with albendazole being preferred over mebendazole, and triple-dose therapy being more effective. Pyrantel pamoate is an alternative. Children 1-2 years receive half the albendazole dose. In pregnant women (2nd/3rd trimester), treatment is beneficial for maternal and perinatal outcomes, and combined anti-helminthic drugs with iron therapy are superior for anemia. For Strongyloides, all infected individuals should be treated. First-line for acute/chronic infection is oral ivermectin (200 µg/kg/day for 2 days). Albendazole (400 mg BID for 7 days with a fatty meal) is an alternative. Patients with HTLV-1 or hyperinfection syndrome require prolonged treatment until larvae are absent from stools or seronegativity is achieved. Parenteral ivermectin (veterinary formulation) may be used for patients unable to take oral medications. Disseminated strongyloidiasis may require combination therapy with albendazole and ivermectin, and hyperinfection with secondary bacterial infections requires parenteral antibiotics; isolation may also be necessary.
section_summaries.prevention: For hookworm, an experimental vaccine to prevent infection and re-infection is under development. Historically, improved urbanization, consistent shoe-wearing, and economic development have been successful in eliminating hookworm as a public health problem in some areas. Specific prevention strategies for Strongyloides are not discussed, though screening at-risk individuals (e.g., those on corticosteroids) is important to prevent severe hyperinfection.
